catalog_quote: [Huber 2013, sec. 4] Tone plays a subordinate role in Ghanaian Pidgin English. It only distinguishes some grammatical morphemes from otherwise homophonous lexical, or less grammaticalized, items: dè prog/hab vs. dé cop, gò fut/cond vs. gó 'go', bì cop vs. bí 'bee'. Tone also distinguishes free, independent pronouns (H, e.g. wí) from bound, dependent ones (L, wì). Ghanaian Pidgin English allows quite complex syllable structures, with up to three consonants in the onset and two in the coda ... [Yakpo 2021] All African English-lexifier creoles make use of grammatical tone. We find identical or similar instantiations of grammatical tone like tone deletion and replacement during compounding and reduplication in Pichi (section 2.1.2), Nigerian Pidgin (Faraclas, 1996, 251–252), Krio (Finney, 1993), Cameroon Pidgin (Nkengasong, 2016, 36–37), and Ghanaian Pidgin (Huber, 2003). ... tone_statements.citation: Steien, Guri Bordal & Kofi Yakpo. 2020. Romancing with tone: On the outcomes of prosodic contact. Language 96(1): 1-41. doi:10.1353/lan.2020.0000
tone_statements.quote: Other works cover aspects of the prosodic systems of ... Ghanaian Pidgin English (Huber 2013). The sources suggest that the prosodic systems of these languages show the characteristic outcomes of stress-to-tone mapping. They have two-tone systems in which most content words of English origin feature an obligatory and culminative H tone, while African-sourced content words show diverse tone patterns, including ones with no H tone at all. [p. 23]

sources.citation: Amoako, Joe K. Y. B. 1992. Ghanaian Pidgin English: in search of diachronic, synchronic, and sociolinguistic evidence. Ph.D. dissertation, University of Florida, 217 pp. (archive.org ghanaianpidginen00amoa).
sources.quote: 'GPE is becoming a tone language because it uses the pitch of individual syllables to contrast meanings in some cases. Native Ghanaian languages, especially Akan, have two main tones, high (H) and low (L) ... The above tone phenomenon of the native Ghanaian languages has been transferred to GPE, e.g.: L go will/shall, H go go; L de they, H de copula; L no negative marker, H no know.' Later: 'Tone is used to bring about lexical as well as grammatical differences in GPE.' No statement on word stress; the word 'stress' does not occur in the phonology chapter.
sources.locator: ch. 'Phonology', section 'Tone', pp. 60-61 (djvu the text); morphology intro p. ~64

sources.citation: Yakpo, Kofi. 2023. The indigenization of Ghanaian Pidgin English. World Englishes 43(1): 182-202. doi:10.1111/weng.12635 (OA offprint, Zenodo 8228598).
sources.quote: 'All Ghanaian languages including Pidgin are tone languages. A high tone is rendered by an acute accent /ó/ and a low tone by a grave accent /ò/.' Body text treats copula forms as distinguished 'by a lexical high tone'. Nothing on word-stress placement.
sources.locator: endnote 2 (offprint p. 17); body pp. 8-11 (tonal minimal pairs yɛ̀ COP vs yɛ́ 'make', bì COP vs bí COP.NFACT)
